plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000065), original: a narrator inherits her great-aunt Vesna's typewriter with a sticking e, chooses a full repair, then recognizes the raised e in Vesna's carbon copies and switches to cleaning only. Topic and names checked against every bank (a recipe-themed inheritance story exists, so that theme was avoided). Ten questions, four aimed at hard. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Lift
passages.text:
The typewriter arrived in a cardboard box that still smelled of my great-aunt Vesna's apartment: lemon oil and radiator dust. My mother had wanted to give it away. I had asked for it before I knew why, and now that it sat on my desk, heavy and green and faintly ridiculous beside my laptop, I was not sure I could explain myself.

The machine worked, mostly. The e stuck. Every time I struck it, the type bar rose, kissed the paper, and hung there a beat too long, so that the next letter landed on top of it unless I waited. Typing a sentence was like walking beside someone who kept stopping to look in shop windows.

Mr. Pellerin's repair shop was a single room above a dry cleaner. He lifted the cover, peered inside, and pressed the e with one thick finger. "Sixty years of oil and dust," he said. "I can clean it. Or I can replace the whole linkage, new spring and new bar, and it will never stick again." He named two prices. The second was three times the first.

I chose the second without much thought. Fixing a thing properly seemed like the respectful choice. Mr. Pellerin nodded, but before I left he rolled a sheet of paper into the machine and typed a line, slowly, letting each e come home. He tore the sheet out and handed it to me. "For comparison," he said. "Afterward."

That night I found Vesna's letters at the bottom of the box: forty years of carbon copies, one for every letter she had sent. I had never read them. I read them now, and halfway through the first one I stopped, because I recognized the e's. Each one sat a hair higher than its neighbors, a small lift in every word, as if the page were breathing. I laid Mr. Pellerin's line beside hers. The same lift. The machine had been doing this for longer than I had been alive.

I called the shop in the morning. Mr. Pellerin did not sound surprised. "Cleaning only, then," he said. "It will still stick a little. You'll learn the rhythm." I said I would. What I did not say, because I did not yet have the words for it, was that I had not really been asking him to fix a machine. I had been asking him to help me keep someone, and I had nearly paid him to erase her.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.A: A narrator chooses, then rejects, a full repair of a great-aunt's typewriter.
choices.B: A narrator learns to repair typewriters from a shop owner and later opens a repair business.
choices.C: A narrator argues with a parent about whether to keep a typewriter and finally gives it away.
choices.D: A narrator discovers that a great-aunt's letters were typed on a different machine entirely.

candidates.evidence: I had been asking him to help me keep someone
candidates.explanation: The narrator first chooses the replacement, then recognizes the machine's raised e in Vesna's letters and switches to cleaning only.

B.rationale: She takes the typewriter to Mr. Pellerin; she does not learn repair or open a business.

C.rationale: Her mother wanted to give it away, but the narrator keeps it, and there is no argument.

D.rationale: The narrator finds that the letters show the same lift as her machine.

hints: What does the narrator decide at the end, and why?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the beginning, the turn, and the end.

candidates.remember: A summary of a narrative must include its turning point.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the second repair option Mr. Pellerin offered would:

choices.C: keep the e from sticking again.
choices.D: take longer than the narrator could wait.

candidates.evidence: and it will never stick again
candidates.explanation: Mr. Pellerin says that replacing the linkage means the key will never stick again.

A.rationale: The second option cost three times the first.

B.rationale: The passage says nothing about its color.

D.rationale: The passage does not mention how long the repair would take.

hints: What did Mr. Pellerin say about the replacement?

strategy.explanation: Find his description of the two options.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: The comparison of typing on the machine to "walking beside someone who kept stopping to look in shop windows" (paragraph 2) mainly suggests that the typing was:

choices.C: too fast for the narrator to control.

candidates.evidence: hung there a beat too long
candidates.explanation: Someone who keeps stopping interrupts a walk again and again, just as the sticking e makes the narrator pause after each one.

A.rationale: The comparison describes a frustrating stop-and-start rhythm, not relaxation.

C.rationale: The key hangs "a beat too long," which slows the typing.

D.rationale: The narrator can type sentences if she waits.

hints: What does the sticking key do to the typing?

strategy.explanation: Match the comparison to the problem it describes.

candidates.remember: Connect a comparison to the literal detail it explains.

candidates.stem: The narrator's statement "Fixing a thing properly seemed like the respectful choice" (paragraph 4) suggests that at that point the narrator believed:

choices.A: Mr. Pellerin would be offended by a choice of the cheaper option.
choices.B: the cleaning option would damage the typewriter further.
choices.C: the narrator's mother expected a costly repair.
choices.D: a full repair would best honor the typewriter and its former owner.

candidates.evidence: Fixing a thing properly seemed like the respectful choice
candidates.explanation: She chose the more complete repair because doing it "properly" seemed respectful, which reflects a belief that full repair would honor the machine and Vesna.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests she was worried about offending him.

B.rationale: She gives no reason to think cleaning would cause damage.

C.rationale: Her mother is not mentioned in connection with the repair.

strategy.explanation: Consider why the object matters to her.

candidates.remember: Infer a belief from the reason a character gives.

candidates.stem: In the passage, the line Mr. Pellerin types before the repair serves mainly to:

choices.A: provide a sample the narrator later matches to Vesna's letters.
choices.B: show that Mr. Pellerin doubted the narrator would pay for the repair.
choices.C: prove that the machine could no longer type legible letters.
choices.D: demonstrate the speed at which Mr. Pellerin could type.

candidates.evidence: I laid Mr. Pellerin's line beside hers
candidates.explanation: The typed line becomes the sample the narrator places beside Vesna's letters, revealing the same raised e.

B.rationale: He types the line "for comparison," not because of doubts about payment.

C.rationale: The narrator can read the line and compare its e's.

D.rationale: He types slowly, letting each e come home.

hints: How does the narrator use the line later?

strategy.explanation: Trace the detail to where it appears again.

candidates.remember: A detail introduced early often matters later in a narrative.

author_checklist.hardness: the detail's role differs from its stated purpose

candidates.stem: Mr. Pellerin's reaction when the narrator calls the shop suggests that he:

choices.A: was disappointed to lose the more expensive repair.
choices.B: believed cleaning would not fix the machine at all.
choices.C: had expected the narrator might keep the quirk.
choices.D: had already started replacing the linkage.

candidates.evidence: Mr. Pellerin did not sound surprised
candidates.explanation: He was not surprised by her change of mind and had given her a sample "for comparison," which suggests he anticipated she might want to keep the quirk.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests disappointment; he simply confirms the cleaning.

B.rationale: He says it will still stick only a little.

D.rationale: He confirms "Cleaning only, then" without mentioning any work begun.

hints: What does "did not sound surprised" imply?

strategy.explanation: Combine his reaction with his earlier action.

candidates.remember: Infer a character's expectations from reactions and earlier actions.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the phrase "come home" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: Mr. Pellerin types slowly so that each sticking type bar can fall back to its resting position, or "settle back into place."

A.rationale: The phrase describes the movement of the type bar, not ownership.

C.rationale: Nothing is arriving at a house.

D.rationale: He types slowly so each e can fall back, not strike harder.

hints: What problem does the e have?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context, not the literal one.

candidates.stem: In the final sentence, the narrator suggests that replacing the linkage would have:

choices.A: insulted Mr. Pellerin by doubting his skill at cleaning.
choices.B: made Vesna's letters impossible for anyone to read.
choices.C: destroyed the carbon copies found in the box.
choices.D: erased a trace of the great-aunt that survived in the machine.

candidates.evidence: I had nearly paid him to erase her
candidates.explanation: The raised e is a mark of Vesna's typing that survives in the machine; replacing the linkage would have erased that link to her.

A.rationale: The narrator does not suggest that replacement would insult him.

B.rationale: The letters were already typed; a repair would not change them.

C.rationale: Repairing the machine would not affect the copies.

strategy.explanation: Connect the last sentence to the discovery in paragraph 5.

candidates.remember: Interpret figurative endings through the details that set them up.

author_checklist.hardness: figurative language tied to an earlier discovery

candidates.stem: The passage indicates that the letters at the bottom of the box were:

choices.A: letters the narrator had once written to Vesna.
choices.B: copies Vesna had kept of letters she sent.
choices.C: drafts of letters Vesna never mailed.
choices.D: notes Mr. Pellerin had left in the machine.

candidates.evidence: forty years of carbon copies, one for every letter she had sent
candidates.explanation: The passage calls them carbon copies of every letter Vesna had sent.

C.rationale: They are copies of letters she sent.

D.rationale: Mr. Pellerin typed one line, which he handed to the narrator.

hints: What kind of letters were they?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: In the first paragraph, the narrator's feelings about having asked for the typewriter are best described as:

choices.A: regretful, since the narrator's mother wanted it.
choices.B: proud, since it matches the laptop.
choices.C: uncertain, since the narrator cannot explain why.
choices.D: indifferent, since it was never meant for use.

candidates.evidence: I was not sure I could explain myself
candidates.explanation: She asked for the typewriter "before I knew why" and is "not sure" she could explain herself, showing uncertainty.

A.rationale: Her mother wanted to give it away, not keep it, and the narrator shows no regret.

B.rationale: She calls it "faintly ridiculous beside my laptop."

D.rationale: She takes it for repair, which shows she means to use it.

hints: What does the narrator say about her reason?

strategy.explanation: Look for words about her own feelings.

candidates.remember: Identify attitude from the narrator's own words.
